claim: The TAM receptor tyrosine kinases Tyro3, Axl, and Mer regulate key features of cellular physiology.
source: The TAM receptor tyrosine kinases Tyro3, Axl, and Mer regulate key features of cellular physiology, yet the differential activities of the TAM ligands Gas6 and Protein S are poorly understood.
evidence: This is a general statement about TAM receptor function that is supported by the broader scientific literature and context of the study.

claim: The differential activities of the TAM ligands Gas6 and Protein S are poorly understood.
source: The TAM receptor tyrosine kinases Tyro3, Axl, and Mer regulate key features of cellular physiology, yet the differential activities of the TAM ligands Gas6 and Protein S are poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: The TAMs segregate into two groups based on ligand specificity, regulation by phosphatidylserine, and function.
source: We have used biochemical and genetic analyses to delineate the rules for TAM receptor–ligand engagement and find that the TAMs segregate into two groups based on ligand specificity, regulation by phosphatidylserine, and function.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including receptor activation assays and genetic analyses.

claim: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both Gas6 and Protein S ligands.
source: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both ligands but only Gas6 activates Axl.
evidence: This is supported by the receptor activation experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Only Gas6 activates Axl.
source: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both ligands but only Gas6 activates Axl.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activation assays in Figure 2D-F showing Axl activation by Gas6 but not Pros1.

claim: Optimal TAM signaling requires coincident TAM ligand engagement of both its receptor and the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer).
source: Optimal TAM signaling requires coincident TAM ligand engagement of both its receptor and the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer): Gas6 lacking its PtdSer-binding 'Gla domain' is significantly weakened as a Tyro3/Mer agonist and is inert as an Axl agonist, even though it binds to Axl with wild-type affinity.
evidence: This is supported by experiments comparing full-length and Gla-less Gas6 in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Gas6 lacking its PtdSer-binding 'Gla domain' is significantly weakened as a Tyro3/Mer agonist.
source: Optimal TAM signaling requires coincident TAM ligand engagement of both its receptor and the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer): Gas6 lacking its PtdSer-binding 'Gla domain' is significantly weakened as a Tyro3/Mer agonist and is inert as an Axl agonist, even though it binds to Axl with wild-type affinity.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the activation assays in Figure 3A and 3C showing reduced activation of Tyro3 and Mer by Gla-less Gas6.

claim: Gas6 lacking its Gla domain is inert as an Axl agonist, even though it binds to Axl with wild-type affinity.
source: Optimal TAM signaling requires coincident TAM ligand engagement of both its receptor and the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer): Gas6 lacking its PtdSer-binding 'Gla domain' is significantly weakened as a Tyro3/Mer agonist and is inert as an Axl agonist, even though it binds to Axl with wild-type affinity.
evidence: This is supported by Figure 3B showing no Axl activation by Gla-less Gas6 and Figure 3E showing equivalent binding affinity.

claim: In two settings of TAM-dependent homeostatic phagocytosis, Mer plays a predominant role while Axl is dispensable.
source: In two settings of TAM-dependent homeostatic phagocytosis, Mer plays a predominant role while Axl is dispensable, and activation of Mer by Protein S is sufficient to drive phagocytosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the genetic analyses in the retina (Figure 7) and testes (Figure 8).

claim: Activation of Mer by Protein S is sufficient to drive phagocytosis.
source: In two settings of TAM-dependent homeostatic phagocytosis, Mer plays a predominant role while Axl is dispensable, and activation of Mer by Protein S is sufficient to drive phagocytosis.
evidence: This is supported by the Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− double mutant analysis in Figures 7 and 8, where only Pros1-Mer signaling remains functional.

claim: TAM signaling regulates the 'homeostatic' or silent phagocytosis of billions of apoptotic cells generated on a daily basis throughout life.
source: In these settings, TAM signaling regulates multiple functions but two are especially prominent. The first is the 'homeostatic' or silent phagocytosis of the billions of apoptotic cells (ACs) that are generated on a daily basis throughout life (Scott et al., 2001; Lemke and Burstyn-Cohen, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TAM signaling regulates the inhibition of the innate immune inflammatory response in dendritic cells, macrophages, and other sentinel cells of the immune system.
source: The second is the inhibition of the innate immune inflammatory response in dendritic cells (DCs), macrophages, and other sentinel cells of the immune system (Rothlin et al., 2007; Lemke and Rothlin, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deficiencies in TAM expression or activity lead to autoimmunity, blindness, and infertility.
source: Deficiencies in TAM expression or activity lead to autoimmunity, blindness, and infertility (Lu et al., 1999; D'Cruz et al., 2000; Lu and Lemke, 2001; Duncan et al., 2003; Lemke and Lu, 2003; Rothlin and Lemke, 2010; Lemke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Over-expression or aberrant activation of Tyro3, Axl, or Mer is associated with the development, progression, and metastasis of cancers.
source: Conversely, over-expression or aberrant activation of Tyro3, Axl, or Mer (gene name Mertk) is associated with the development, progression, and metastasis of cancers (Avilla et al., 2011; Cummings et al., 2013; Lemke, 2013; Meyer et al., 2013; Paccez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Axl mediates the resistance of solid tumors and leukemias to EGFR-directed chemotherapeutic agents.
source: Axl in particular has been shown to mediate the resistance of solid tumors and leukemias to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-directed chemotherapeutic agents (Hong et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2012; Meyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Elevated TAM expression has been implicated in increased susceptibility to infection by enveloped viruses.
source: Elevated TAM expression has also recently been implicated in increased susceptibility to infection by enveloped viruses (Shimojima et al., 2006; Morizono et al., 2011; Meertens et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gas6 is thought to function as a ligand for all three TAM receptors.
source: Gas6 is thought to function as a ligand for all three receptors (Stitt et al., 1995; Nagata et al., 1996; Chen et al., 1997), but the role of Pros1 as a ligand for one or more TAM receptors has until recently been controversial (Godowski et al., 1995; Anderson et al., 2003; Hafizi and Dahlback, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The role of Pros1 as a ligand for one or more TAM receptors has until recently been controversial.
source: Gas6 is thought to function as a ligand for all three receptors (Stitt et al., 1995; Nagata et al., 1996; Chen et al., 1997), but the role of Pros1 as a ligand for one or more TAM receptors has until recently been controversial (Godowski et al., 1995; Anderson et al., 2003; Hafizi and Dahlback, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature indicating conflicting findings.

claim: Gas6 and Pros1 have a C-terminal 'SHBG domain' that binds to the Ig-like domains of TAM receptors.
source: At the same time, the unique structural features of Gas6 and Pros1—in which a C-terminal 'SHBG domain' binds to the Ig-like domains of TAM receptors while an N-terminal γ-carboxylated 'Gla domain' binds, in a Ca2+-dependent reaction, to the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) (Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Lemke, 2013)—have led to conflicting conclusions as to the relative importance of these two domains in receptor binding vs activation (Mark et al., 1996; Nakano et al., 1997; Tanabe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing the structural features.

claim: Gas6 and Pros1 have an N-terminal γ-carboxylated 'Gla domain' that binds, in a Ca2+-dependent reaction, to the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer).
source: At the same time, the unique structural features of Gas6 and Pros1—in which a C-terminal 'SHBG domain' binds to the Ig-like domains of TAM receptors while an N-terminal γ-carboxylated 'Gla domain' binds, in a Ca2+-dependent reaction, to the phospholipid phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) (Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Lemke, 2013)—have led to conflicting conclusions as to the relative importance of these two domains in receptor binding vs activation (Mark et al., 1996; Nakano et al., 1997; Tanabe et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature describing the structural features.

claim: Gas6 and Pros1 binding to the PtdSer-containing membranes of enveloped viruses potentiates TAM activation.
source: Although Gas6 and Pros1 binding to the PtdSer-containing membranes of enveloped viruses potentiates TAM activation (Meertens et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), and the Gla domain is thought to be required to 'bridge' a TAM receptor expressed on the surface of a phagocyte to the PtdSer expressed on the surface of its AC target (Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Lemke and Burstyn-Cohen, 2010; Nagata et al., 2010), a preparation of recombinant mouse Gas6 that lacks the Gla domain entirely is sold commercially as a TAM activator.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The Gla domain is thought to be required to 'bridge' a TAM receptor expressed on the surface of a phagocyte to the PtdSer expressed on the surface of its AC target.
source: Although Gas6 and Pros1 binding to the PtdSer-containing membranes of enveloped viruses potentiates TAM activation (Meertens et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), and the Gla domain is thought to be required to 'bridge' a TAM receptor expressed on the surface of a phagocyte to the PtdSer expressed on the surface of its AC target (Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Lemke and Burstyn-Cohen, 2010; Nagata et al., 2010), a preparation of recombinant mouse Gas6 that lacks the Gla domain entirely is sold commercially as a TAM activator.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A preparation of recombinant mouse Gas6 that lacks the Gla domain entirely is sold commercially as a TAM activator.
source: Although Gas6 and Pros1 binding to the PtdSer-containing membranes of enveloped viruses potentiates TAM activation (Meertens et al., 2012; Bhattacharyya et al., 2013), and the Gla domain is thought to be required to 'bridge' a TAM receptor expressed on the surface of a phagocyte to the PtdSer expressed on the surface of its AC target (Lemke and Rothlin, 2008; Lemke and Burstyn-Cohen, 2010; Nagata et al., 2010), a preparation of recombinant mouse Gas6 that lacks the Gla domain entirely is sold commercially as a TAM activator.
evidence: This is a factual statement about commercial availability.

claim: Potentially distinct roles for Pros1 and Gas6 in vivo have only recently begun to be appreciated.
source: Potentially distinct roles for Pros1 and Gas6 in vivo have only recently begun to be appreciated (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012; Carrera Silva et al., 2013), and to date only a single genetic study of the importance of Gas6 vs Pros1 in a TAM-dependent process has been reported (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: To date only a single genetic study of the importance of Gas6 vs Pros1 in a TAM-dependent process has been reported.
source: Potentially distinct roles for Pros1 and Gas6 in vivo have only recently begun to be appreciated (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012; Carrera Silva et al., 2013), and to date only a single genetic study of the importance of Gas6 vs Pros1 in a TAM-dependent process has been reported (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: TAM signaling during the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments by retinal pigment epithelial cells requires Mer.
source: This study addressed TAM signaling during the phagocytosis of photoreceptor (PR) outer segments by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Strauss, 2005), which express Mer and Tyro3 but no Axl (Prasad et al., 2006). RPE phagocytosis of the PtdSer-displaying tips of PR outer segments (Ruggiero et al., 2012) requires Mer—mice, rats, and humans that carry loss-of-function mutations in the Mertk gene are blind, due to the cell-non-autonomous degeneration of nearly all PRs (D'Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000; Duncan et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2006; Mackay et al., 2010; Nandrot and Dufour, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: RPE cells express Mer and Tyro3 but no Axl.
source: This study addressed TAM signaling during the phagocytosis of photoreceptor (PR) outer segments by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Strauss, 2005), which express Mer and Tyro3 but no Axl (Prasad et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice, rats, and humans that carry loss-of-function mutations in the Mertk gene are blind, due to the cell-non-autonomous degeneration of nearly all PRs.
source: RPE phagocytosis of the PtdSer-displaying tips of PR outer segments (Ruggiero et al., 2012) requires Mer—mice, rats, and humans that carry loss-of-function mutations in the Mertk gene are blind, due to the cell-non-autonomous degeneration of nearly all PRs (D'Cruz et al., 2000; Gal et al., 2000; Duncan et al., 2003; Prasad et al., 2006; Mackay et al., 2010; Nandrot and Dufour, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Retinal loss of either the mouse Gas6 or Pros1 gene alone yields a retina with a normal number of PRs.
source: Retinal loss of either the mouse Gas6 or Pros1 gene alone yields a retina with a normal number of PRs, but the combined loss of Pros1 and Gas6 results in a PR degeneration phenotype that fully phenocopies the cell death seen in Mertk−/− mice (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The combined loss of Pros1 and Gas6 results in a PR degeneration phenotype that fully phenocopies the cell death seen in Mertk−/− mice.
source: Retinal loss of either the mouse Gas6 or Pros1 gene alone yields a retina with a normal number of PRs, but the combined loss of Pros1 and Gas6 results in a PR degeneration phenotype that fully phenocopies the cell death seen in Mertk−/− mice (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Pros1 is sufficient to drive Mer-dependent phagocytosis in RPE cells.
source: While this analysis demonstrated that Pros1 is sufficient to drive Mer-dependent phagocytosis in RPE cells, the presence of Tyro3 in these cells raised the possibility that Pros1 activation of the Mer kinase might be dependent on Pros1 binding to Tyro3.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature and the genetic analysis in this study.

claim: All recombinant mouse ligands ran as single bands under reducing conditions on SDS polyacrylamide gels.
source: All recombinant mouse ligands ran as single bands under reducing conditions on SDS polyacrylamide gels and eluted from an anion exchange column as a single peak suggesting that the ligands were pure (Figure 1A and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image in Figure 1A.

claim: Recombinant mouse ligands eluted from an anion exchange column as a single peak suggesting that the ligands were pure.
source: All recombinant mouse ligands ran as single bands under reducing conditions on SDS polyacrylamide gels and eluted from an anion exchange column as a single peak suggesting that the ligands were pure (Figure 1A and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on chromatography data.

claim: Commercially available Protein S purified from human plasma ran as a single predominant band under reducing conditions, together with a secondary band of lower molecular weight.
source: Commercially available Protein S purified from human plasma (hPros1) ran as a single predominant band under reducing conditions, together with a secondary band of lower molecular weight (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the gel image in Figure 1A.

claim: Full-length Gas6 in solution is a mixture of monomers, dimers, and/or higher order multimers.
source: Size exclusion chromatography suggested that full-length Gas6 in solution is a mixture of monomers, dimers, and/or higher order multimers, whereas the Gla-less form appeared as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gla-less Gas6 appeared as a monomer in size exclusion chromatography.
source: Size exclusion chromatography suggested that full-length Gas6 in solution is a mixture of monomers, dimers, and/or higher order multimers, whereas the Gla-less form appeared as a monomer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the size exclusion chromatography data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: hPros1 forms disulfide-linked multimers, and multimerization is enhanced by apoptotic cells.
source: These elution profiles are consistent with earlier work on hPros1, indicating that it forms disulfide-linked multimers, and that multimerization is enhanced by apoptotic cells (Uehara and Shacter, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: All established cell lines analyzed express at least one TAM receptor.
source: All established cell lines we have analyzed express at least one TAM receptor.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Both purified human and recombinant mouse Pros1 are capable of rapidly activating Tyro3 autophosphorylation.
source: We found that both purified human and recombinant mouse Pros1 (hPros1 and rmPros1, respectively) were capable of rapidly activating Tyro3 autophosphorylation (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Purified hPros1 was more stable biochemically and often more potent than rmPros1.
source: In our hands, purified hPros1 was more stable biochemically and often more potent than rmPros1 (Figure 2A), and we therefore used the human protein for the majority of the Pros1 experiments described below.
evidence: This is based on comparative experimental observations shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Both mouse and human Pros1 are active as ligands for a chimeric receptor comprised of the mouse Tyro3 ectodomain linked to the cytoplasmic domain of the R1 chain of the interferon-gamma receptor.
source: Consistent with these observations, both mouse and human Pros1 were also recently found to be active as ligands for a chimeric receptor comprised of the mouse Tyro3 ectodomain linked to the cytoplasmic domain of the R1 chain of the interferon (IFN)-gamma (γ) receptor (Tsou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mouse Tyro3 is strongly activated by rmGas6.
source: Mouse Tyro3 was also strongly activated by rmGas6 (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Mouse Axl can only be activated by rmGas6.
source: In contrast, we found that mouse Axl could only be activated by rmGas6 (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2D-F showing Axl activation by Gas6 but not Pros1.

claim: Axl activation is detected at rmGas6 concentrations as low as 1 nM.
source: While we detected 10 min activation of Axl at rmGas6 concentrations as low as 1 nM (Figure 2D), we could not detect Axl activation by either mouse Pros1 (Figure 2E) or human Pros1 (Figure 2F) at any concentration tested.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2D.

claim: Axl activation by mouse Pros1 or human Pros1 could not be detected at any concentration tested.
source: While we detected 10 min activation of Axl at rmGas6 concentrations as low as 1 nM (Figure 2D), we could not detect Axl activation by either mouse Pros1 (Figure 2E) or human Pros1 (Figure 2F) at any concentration tested.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2E and 2F.

claim: hGas6 but not mPros1 induces STAT1 phosphorylation downstream of a chimeric mAxl/γR1 receptor expressed in CHO cells.
source: Correspondingly, hGas6 but not mPros1 has been found to induce STAT1 phosphorylation downstream of a chimeric mAxl/γR1 receptor expressed in CHO cells (Tsou et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Both rmGas6 and hPros1 are capable of activating Mer in Mer-expressing MEFs.
source: We found that both ligands were capable of activating this receptor in Mer-expressing MEFs, but that rmGas6 was more potent than hPros1 in this assay (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2G.

claim: rmGas6 is more potent than hPros1 in activating Mer in Mer-expressing MEFs.
source: We found that both ligands were capable of activating this receptor in Mer-expressing MEFs, but that rmGas6 was more potent than hPros1 in this assay (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2G.

claim: Both rmGas6 and hPros1/rmPros1 function as a ligand for Mer in dexamethasone-treated mouse bone marrow-derived macrophages.
source: We found that both rmGas6 and hPros1/rmPros1 also function as a ligand for Mer in these cells (Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 2H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: γ-carboxylation of glutamic acid is required for the Ca2+-dependent binding of Gla domains to PtdSer.
source: Together with several components of the blood coagulation cascade, including prothrombin, Protein C, and factors VII, IX, and X, both Gas6 and Pros1 carry 'Gla domains'—polypeptide segments of ∼45 amino acids that contain clusters of 10–12 glutamic acid residues whose gamma carbons are post-translationally carboxylated in a vitamin K-dependent reaction (Stitt et al., 1995; Nelsestuen et al., 2000; Huang et al., 2003; Bandyopadhyay, 2008). This γ-carboxylation of glutamic acid is required for the Ca2+-dependent binding of Gla domains to PtdSer, which is displayed on the surface of apoptotic cells (ACs) and enveloped viruses (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: γ-carboxylation is indispensible for the bioactivity of the Gla domain-containing proteins of the coagulation cascade.
source: It is indispensible for the bioactivity of the Gla domain-containing proteins of the coagulation cascade and is a principal reason that vitamin K is an essential vitamin (Freedman et al., 1995; Ishimoto et al., 2000; Bandyopadhyay, 2008; Rajotte et al., 2008; Lemke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The anticoagulant warfarin and related blood thinners antagonize vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of Gla domains.
source: The anticoagulant warfarin and related blood thinners antagonize vitamin K-dependent γ-carboxylation of Gla domains (Stafford, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Full-length Gas6 is markedly (~20-fold) more potent than Gla-less rmGas6 in activating Tyro3.
source: We found that although both full-length and Gla-less rmGas6 were capable of activating Tyro3, the full-length protein was markedly (∼20-fold) more potent (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 3A.

claim: Full-length Gas6 is a very potent Axl ligand.
source: When we performed this same comparison for Axl-expressing MEFs, we observed an even stronger dependence. Full-length Gas6 was a very potent Axl ligand (Figure 3B, left 6 lanes), but the Gla-less version was incapable of activating Axl at any concentration tested (up to 750 nM; Figure 3B, right 6 lanes).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: Gla-less Gas6 is incapable of activating Axl at any concentration tested (up to 750 nM).
source: When we performed this same comparison for Axl-expressing MEFs, we observed an even stronger dependence. Full-length Gas6 was a very potent Axl ligand (Figure 3B, left 6 lanes), but the Gla-less version was incapable of activating Axl at any concentration tested (up to 750 nM; Figure 3B, right 6 lanes).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 3B.

claim: Full-length Gas6 is ~20-fold more potent than Gla-less Gas6 in activating Mer in Mer-expressing Dex-Mϕ.
source: When we compared the ability of full-length and Gla-less rmGas6 to activate Mer in Mer-expressing Dex-Mϕ, we observed a pattern similar to that seen for Tyro3. Although both forms of the ligand were capable of activating Mer, full-length Gas6 was ∼20-fold more potent than its Gla-less counterpart (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: The TAM receptors fall into two groups based on features of their ligand and PtdSer activation profiles: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both Gas6 and Pros1, whereas Axl is activated only by Gas6.
source: Thus, the TAM receptors fall into two groups based on features of their ligand and PtdSer activation profiles: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both Gas6 and Pros1, whereas Axl is activated only by Gas6; and while Gla-less Gas6 is a substantially weaker ligand for Tyro3 and Mer, it is effectively dead as a ligand for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Gla-less Gas6 is a substantially weaker ligand for Tyro3 and Mer, but is effectively dead as a ligand for Axl.
source: Thus, the TAM receptors fall into two groups based on features of their ligand and PtdSer activation profiles: Tyro3 and Mer are activated by both Gas6 and Pros1, whereas Axl is activated only by Gas6; and while Gla-less Gas6 is a substantially weaker ligand for Tyro3 and Mer, it is effectively dead as a ligand for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: The difference in the ability of Gla-less Gas6 to activate Axl vs Tyro3/Mer is unrelated to any difference in the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the three receptors.
source: The difference in the ability of Gla-less Gas6 to activate Axl vs Tyro3/Mer is unrelated to any difference in the intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity of the three receptors.
evidence: This is supported by the chimeric receptor experiment in Figure 3D.

claim: A Tyro3–Axl chimeric receptor composed of the Tyro3 extracellular domain linked to the Axl tyrosine kinase displays diminished activation by Gla-less Gas6 similar to that seen with Tyro3.
source: We found that a Tyro3–Axl chimeric receptor composed of the Tyro3 extracellular domain linked to the Axl tyrosine kinase, when expressed in TAM TKO MEFs, displayed diminished activation by Gla-less Gas6 similar to that seen with Tyro3 (Figure 3A,D).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 3A and 3D.

claim: The interaction of Gla-less Gas6 to Tyro3 and Mer is distinct structurally from its interaction with Axl.
source: This suggests that the interaction of Gla-less Gas6 to Tyro3 and Mer is distinct structurally from its interaction with Axl.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimeric receptor experiment.

claim: The Gas6 Gla domain is required for optimal activation of Tyro3 and Mer, and this requirement is absolute for Axl.
source: Together, these results indicate that the Gas6 Gla domain is required for optimal activation of Tyro3 and Mer, and that this requirement is absolute for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Full-length and Gla-less Gas6 display essentially the same IC50 for Axl binding—approximately 0.7 nM.
source: We found that full-length and Gla-less Gas6 displayed essentially the same IC50 for Axl binding—approximately 0.7 nM in this assay (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by the binding assay data in Figure 3E.

claim: The inability of Gla-less Gas6 to activate Axl is unrelated to its ability to bind the receptor.
source: Thus, the inability of Gla-less Gas6 to activate Axl is unrelated to its ability to bind the receptor; and conversely, the ability of a Gas6 variant to bind Axl is unrelated to its ability to activate the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and activation data in Figure 3.

claim: The ability of a Gas6 variant to bind Axl is unrelated to its ability to activate the receptor.
source: Thus, the inability of Gla-less Gas6 to activate Axl is unrelated to its ability to bind the receptor; and conversely, the ability of a Gas6 variant to bind Axl is unrelated to its ability to activate the receptor.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and activation data in Figure 3.

claim: A crystal structure of the Axl ectodomain bound to Gla-less Gas6 represents a ligand-occupied but inactive Axl configuration.
source: These properties suggest that a crystal structure of the Axl ectodomain bound to Gla-less Gas6 (Sasaki et al., 2006) represents a ligand-occupied but inactive Axl configuration.
evidence: This is inferred from the binding and activation data, with reference to a prior structural study.

claim: Gas6 appears to be specifically and constitutively bound to Axl without significant activation of the receptor in tissues in vivo.
source: In related work, we have found that these properties are also exceptionally important to Gas6–Axl binding and signaling in tissues in vivo, where Gas6 appears to be specifically and constitutively bound to Axl without significant activation of the receptor (Zagórska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to related work.

claim: No binding of Pros1 to Axl-expressing MEFs was detected.
source: Consistent with the failure of Pros1 to activate Axl in culture (Figure 2E,F), we detected no binding of Pros1 to Axl-expressing MEFs (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation.

claim: Annexin A5 antagonized Gas6 activation of Tyro3 in Tyro3_TAM TKO MEFs.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, we found that the PtdSer-binding protein Annexin A5 antagonized Gas6 activation of Tyro3 in Tyro3_TAM TKO MEFs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 4A.

claim: Significant numbers of pSIVA+PI− apoptotic cells and pSIVA+PI+ late apoptotic/necrotic cells are present in MEF culture medium.
source: We detected significant number of pSIVA+PI− apoptotic cells and pSIVA+PI+ late apoptotic/necrotic cells in the culture medium and even a measurable number of pSIVA+PI− and pSIVA+PI+ cells in the adherent MEFs on the plate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: There are PtdSer-displaying membranes present in the MEF cultures.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that there are PtdSer-displaying membranes present in the MEF cultures.
evidence: This is inferred from the flow cytometry data in Figure 4B.

claim: The molecular weight of PtdSer is ~385 g/mol, while Gas6 and Pros1 have molecular weights of ~80,000 g/mol.
source: It is important to note that the molecular weight of PtdSer is ∼385 g/mol, while Gas6 and Pros1 have molecular weights of ∼80,000 g/mol, and that the crystal structure of the prothrombin Gla domain bound to lyso-PtdSer contains only a single molecule of this phospholipid (Huang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on known molecular weights and citation to structural data.

claim: The crystal structure of the prothrombin Gla domain bound to lyso-PtdSer contains only a single molecule of this phospholipid.
source: It is important to note that the molecular weight of PtdSer is ∼385 g/mol, while Gas6 and Pros1 have molecular weights of ∼80,000 g/mol, and that the crystal structure of the prothrombin Gla domain bound to lyso-PtdSer contains only a single molecule of this phospholipid (Huang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior structural study.

claim: A relatively low level of PtdSer can easily be in molar excess over the Gla domain-containing proteins with which it interacts.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The addition of PtdSer-displaying apoptotic cells markedly shifts the dose–response curves for Pros1 activation of Mer and Gas6 activation of Axl/Mer to lower ligand concentrations.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Binding of rmGas6 to the surface of Axl-expressing MEFs was readily observed at 90 min after application at 4°C.

evidence: This is supported by the immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C.

claim: Binding of rmGas6 to Axl-expressing MEFs was unaffected by the inclusion of 10 mM EDTA.
source: We found that it is not: binding of rmGas6 (at 25 nM) to the surface of Axl-expressing MEFs was readily observed with an anti-Gas6 antibody at 90 min after application (at 4°C), and this binding was unaffected by the inclusion of 10 mM EDTA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C.

claim: Equivalent binding of Gla-less Gas6 to Axl-expressing MEFs was detected.
source: We also detected equivalent binding of Gla-less Gas6 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by the immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4C.

claim: No Gas6 binding was detected in TAM TKO MEFs.
source: In control experiments, no Gas6 binding was detected in TAM TKO MEFs (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by the immunocytochemistry data in Figure 4D.

claim: The observed Gas6 binding is via SHBG domain binding to Axl and not via Gla domain binding to any PtdSer expressed by the MEFs.
source: These results argue that the observed Gas6 binding is via SHBG domain binding to Axl and not via Gla domain binding to any PtdSer expressed by the MEFs.
evidence: This is inferred from the EDTA and Gla-less Gas6 binding experiments.

claim: Gas6 bound to Axl in the presence of EDTA is not capable of activating Axl.
source: We then asked whether Gas6 bound to Axl in the presence of EDTA (Figure 4C, third panel) is capable of activating Axl. We found that it is not: although 10 nM rmGas6 resulted in strong Axl activation in the absence of EDTA, the inclusion of 2, 10, or 50 mM EDTA all blocked this activation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 4E.

claim: The inclusion of 2, 10, or 50 mM EDTA all blocked Gas6 activation of Axl.
source: We found that it is not: although 10 nM rmGas6 resulted in strong Axl activation in the absence of EDTA, the inclusion of 2, 10, or 50 mM EDTA all blocked this activation (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 4E.

claim: The binding of full-length Gas6 alone, in the absence of simultaneous Ca2+-dependent binding of its Gla domain to PtdSer, is insufficient to trigger Axl activation.
source: These results indicate that the binding of full-length Gas6 alone, in the absence of simultaneous Ca2+-dependent binding of its Gla domain to PtdSer, is insufficient to trigger Axl activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the EDTA experiments in Figure 4.

claim: By 30 min after IV injection, equally strong binding of both full-length and Gla-less rmGas6 to F4/80+ red pulp macrophages was observed.
source: By 30 min after IV injection, we observed equally strong binding of both full-length and Gla-less rmGas6 to these cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by the immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5A.

claim: Axl immunoprecipitated 30 min after IV injection of full-length Gas6 was strongly activated.
source: However, this equivalent in vivo binding was not reflected in equivalent Axl activation. When we immunoprecipitated Axl from the spleen 30 min after IV injection of full-length Gas6, we observed that Axl was strongly activated (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: Axl immunoprecipitated after injection of Gla-less rmGas6 showed zero activation.
source: In marked contrast, Axl immunoprecipitated after injection of Gla-less rmGas6 showed zero activation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: Equivalent amounts of full-length and Gla-less Gas6 could be recovered from the spleen after IV injection.
source: This was in spite of the fact that equivalent amounts of full-length and Gla-less Gas6 could be recovered from the spleen (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: The PtdSer required for activation of Axl by full-length rmGas6 injected IV is presumably provided by both apoptotic cells and circulating PtdSer-exposing microparticles.
source: The PtdSer required for activation of Axl by full-length rmGas6 injected IV is presumably provided by both apoptotic cells and circulating PtdSer-exposing microparticles, derived from platelets, erythrocytes, leukocytes, and endothelial cells, which are abundant in the blood (Lacroix and Dignat-George, 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the in vivo experiments and supported by citation to prior literature on microparticles.

claim: The distinct receptor–ligand activation profiles reflect differences that are intrinsic to the Ig-like domains of the TAM ectodomains.
source: We found that the distinct receptor–ligand activation profiles described above reflect differences that are intrinsic to the Ig-like domains of the TAM ectodomains.
evidence: This is supported by the chimeric receptor experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The activation profiles of both rmGas6 and hPros1 are similar for MEF lines expressing equivalent levels of wild-type Tyro3 or the chimeric Tyro3–Axl hybrid.
source: The activation profiles of both rmGas6 (Figure 6C) and hPros1 (Figure 6D) were similar for MEF lines expressing equivalent levels of wild-type Tyro3 or the chimeric Tyro3–Axl hybrid.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 6C and 6D.

claim: Specificity resides within the two N-terminal Ig-like domains of the TAM receptors, and both of these domains are required.
source: We found that specificity resides within the two N-terminal Ig-like domains of the receptors, and that both of these domains are required: a hybrid receptor composed of the two Ig-like domains of Tyro3 linked to the remaining domains of Axl (Figure 6A) was, like Tyro3, potently activated by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 5–8), whereas a chimera that contained only the first Ig-like domain of Tyro3 (Figure 6A) was refractory to activation by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 6D.

claim: A hybrid receptor composed of the two Ig-like domains of Tyro3 linked to the remaining domains of Axl was, like Tyro3, potently activated by Pros1.
source: We found that specificity resides within the two N-terminal Ig-like domains of the receptors, and that both of these domains are required: a hybrid receptor composed of the two Ig-like domains of Tyro3 linked to the remaining domains of Axl (Figure 6A) was, like Tyro3, potently activated by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 5–8), whereas a chimera that contained only the first Ig-like domain of Tyro3 (Figure 6A) was refractory to activation by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 6D.

claim: A chimera that contained only the first Ig-like domain of Tyro3 was refractory to activation by Pros1.
source: We found that specificity resides within the two N-terminal Ig-like domains of the receptors, and that both of these domains are required: a hybrid receptor composed of the two Ig-like domains of Tyro3 linked to the remaining domains of Axl (Figure 6A) was, like Tyro3, potently activated by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 5–8), whereas a chimera that contained only the first Ig-like domain of Tyro3 (Figure 6A) was refractory to activation by Pros1 (Figure 6D, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 6D.

claim: The intrinsic catalytic activity of Axl and Tyro3 are stimulated to comparable levels by ligand binding to the Tyro3 extracellular domain.
source: These results indicate that the intrinsic catalytic activity of Axl and Tyro3 are stimulated to comparable levels by ligand binding—of either Gas6 or Pros1–to the Tyro3 extracellular domain.
evidence: This is inferred from the chimeric receptor experiments in Figure 6.

claim: The Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− ONL is of wild-type thickness.
source: We found that the Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− ONL is also of wild-type thickness (Figure 7A, fifth panel). Thus, Pros1–Mer signaling alone is sufficient to mediate apparently normal phagocytosis in the retina.
evidence: This is supported by the histology data in Figure 7A.

claim: Pros1–Mer signaling alone is sufficient to mediate apparently normal phagocytosis in the retina.
source: We found that the Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− ONL is also of wild-type thickness (Figure 7A, fifth panel). Thus, Pros1–Mer signaling alone is sufficient to mediate apparently normal phagocytosis in the retina.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic analysis in Figure 7A.

claim: Purified Pros1 induces Mer autophosphorylation in the RPE directly, in the absence of any other TAM receptor.
source: As shown in Figure 7B (upper two panels), we demonstrate that purified Pros1 can also activate Tyro3 in this preparation and can activate Mer in both wild-type and Tyro3−/− RPE cells (Figure 7B, lower two panels). Thus, Pros1 induces Mer autophosphorylation in the RPE directly, in the absence of any other TAM receptor, and this Pros1-to-Mer activation alone is sufficient to maintain a normal number of PRs in the retina in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 7B.

claim: Pros1-to-Mer activation alone is sufficient to maintain a normal number of PRs in the retina in vivo.
source: Thus, Pros1 induces Mer autophosphorylation in the RPE directly, in the absence of any other TAM receptor, and this Pros1-to-Mer activation alone is sufficient to maintain a normal number of PRs in the retina in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and biochemical analyses in Figure 7.

claim: Sertoli cells express all three TAM receptors and both ligands.
source: Sertoli cells express all three TAM receptors and both ligands (Lu et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2009), and Tyro3/Axl/Mer triple mouse mutants are infertile due to the toxic accumulation of ACs (Lu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tyro3/Axl/Mer triple mouse mutants are infertile due to the toxic accumulation of ACs.
source: Sertoli cells express all three TAM receptors and both ligands (Lu et al., 1999; Chen et al., 2009), and Tyro3/Axl/Mer triple mouse mutants are infertile due to the toxic accumulation of ACs (Lu et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The major receptor required for Sertoli cell phagocytosis of apoptotic germ cells in the mouse testis is Mer.
source: We found that the major receptor required for Sertoli cell phagocytosis of apoptotic germ cells in the mouse testis is Mer (Figure 8A,B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis of apoptotic cells in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tyro3−/−, Axl−/−, and Gas6−/− single mutant mice all display wild-type number of cCasp3+ ACs (~0.02 cells per tubule cross-section).
source: While Tyro3−/−, Axl−/−, and Gas6−/− single mutant mice all displayed wild-type number of cCasp3+ ACs—∼0.02 cells per tubule cross-section (Figure 8A, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)–Mertk−/− mice displayed nearly 20 times more (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mertk−/− mice display nearly 20 times more cCasp3+ ACs than wild-type.
source: While Tyro3−/−, Axl−/−, and Gas6−/− single mutant mice all displayed wild-type number of cCasp3+ ACs—∼0.02 cells per tubule cross-section (Figure 8A, and Figure 8—figure supplement 1)–Mertk−/− mice displayed nearly 20 times more (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8B.

claim: The number of ACs was not increased in Mertk−/−Axl−/− double knock-outs compared to Mertk−/− single knock-outs in the testis.
source: In contrast to other tissues we have analyzed (e.g., the spleen), the number of ACs was not increased in Mertk−/−Axl−/− double knock-outs compared to Mertk−/− single knock-outs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tyro3−/−Axl−/− double knock-outs display wild-type number of ACs in the testes.
source: More tellingly, Tyro3−/−Axl−/− double knock-outs displayed wild-type number of ACs in the testes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,C), and this was also the case for Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− double knock-outs, in which the only possible TAM signaling axis is Pros1 to Mer (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− double knock-outs display wild-type number of ACs in the testes.
source: More tellingly, Tyro3−/−Axl−/− double knock-outs displayed wild-type number of ACs in the testes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,C), and this was also the case for Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− double knock-outs, in which the only possible TAM signaling axis is Pros1 to Mer (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8B.

claim: Tyro3−/−Mertk−/− double mutants display substantially more ACs in the testis (~2 cCasp3+ cells per each tubule cross-section) than Mertk−/− single mutants.
source: In contrast to the retina, we observed a significant effect of Tyro3 mutation in the presence of an existing Mertk mutation: Tyro3−/−Mertk−/− double mutants displayed substantially more ACs in the testis (∼2 cCasp3+ cells per each tubule cross-section) than did Mertk−/− single mutants (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Combining all three receptor knock-outs in Tyro3−/−Axl−/−Mertk−/− triple mutants led to a massive accumulation of ACs and cCasp3+ material that made accurate counting of ACs impossible.
source: Combining all three receptor knock-outs in Tyro3−/−Axl−/−Mertk−/− triple mutants led to a massive accumulation of ACs and cCasp3+ material that made accurate counting of ACs impossible (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by the histology data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the absence of Mer and Tyro3, Axl can also mediate AC phagocytosis in the testis.
source: This suggests that in the absence of Mer and Tyro3, Axl can also mediate AC phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of Tyro3−/−Mertk−/− double mutants and TAM TKO triple mutants.

claim: The Prosfl/−Gas6−/− testes contain a wild-type number of ACs.
source: Finally, we examined the effect of removing all Gas6 and half the normal Pros1 throughout the mouse and found that the Prosfl/−Gas6−/− testes also contained a wild-type number of ACs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In both the testes and the retina, only half the normal level of only a single TAM ligand (Pros1) is sufficient to maintain an essential level of TAM-dependent phagocytosis.
source: Thus in both the testes and the retina (Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2012), only half the normal level of only a single TAM ligand (Pros1) is sufficient to maintain an essential level of TAM-dependent phagocytosis.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic analyses in the testes and retina, with citation to prior work.

claim: All three TAM receptors are detectable by western blot in the testis.
source: All three TAM receptors are detectable by western blot in the testis (Figure 8C), and there was no significant compensatory change in Tyro3, Axl, or Mer expression in Mertk−/−, Tyro3−/−, Gas6−/−, or Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 8C.

claim: There was no significant compensatory change in Tyro3, Axl, or Mer expression in Mertk−/−, Tyro3−/−, Gas6−/−, or Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− mice in the testis.
source: All three TAM receptors are detectable by western blot in the testis (Figure 8C), and there was no significant compensatory change in Tyro3, Axl, or Mer expression in Mertk−/−, Tyro3−/−, Gas6−/−, or Tyro3−/−Gas6−/− mice (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data in Figure 8C.

claim: The relative protein expression level of TAM receptors in the testis is Mer > Tyro3 > Axl.
source: We used comparative signal intensities on Licor immunoblots of lysates from testis and TAM TKO MEFs expressing HA-tagged Tyro3, Axl, and Mer (Figure 8D) to determine that the relative protein expression level of TAM receptors in the testis is Mer > Tyro3 > Axl (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative western blot analysis in Figure 8D and 8E.

claim: The number of cCasp3+ cells in wild-type vs Tyro3−/−Mertk−/− mice is the same at 10–12 weeks and 9–12 months.
source: Finally, we confirmed that the phenotypes we analyzed at 10–12 weeks were fully developed by this time. We measured the number of cCasp3+ cells in wild-type vs Tyro3−/−Mertk−/− mice at 10–12 weeks vs 9–12 months and saw that this number was the same in both the young and aged testis (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the quantitative analysis in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Mer is the major facilitator of steady-state homeostatic phagocytosis in both the retina and the testis.
source: Together, these results indicate that Mer is the major facilitator of steady-state homeostatic phagocytosis in both the retina and the testis, and that binding and activation of this receptor by Pros1 alone at only half its normal gene dose is sufficient to maintain normal levels of phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic analyses in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Binding and activation of Mer by Pros1 alone at only half its normal gene dose is sufficient to maintain normal levels of phagocytosis in the retina and testis.
source: Together, these results indicate that Mer is the major facilitator of steady-state homeostatic phagocytosis in both the retina and the testis, and that binding and activation of this receptor by Pros1 alone at only half its normal gene dose is sufficient to maintain normal levels of phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic analyses in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: Gas6 alone is capable of binding to and activating Tyro3, Axl, and Mer when these receptors are expressed in isolation.
source: First, Gas6 alone is capable of binding to and activating Tyro3, Axl, and Mer when these receptors are expressed in isolation and is especially potent as a ligand for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Gas6 is especially potent as a ligand for Axl.
source: First, Gas6 alone is capable of binding to and activating Tyro3, Axl, and Mer when these receptors are expressed in isolation and is especially potent as a ligand for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Pros1 alone is capable of binding to and activating Tyro3 and Mer but does not function as a ligand for Axl.
source: Second, Pros1 alone is capable of binding to and activating Tyro3 and Mer but does not function as a ligand for Axl.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The PtdSer-binding Gla domain of Gas6, PtdSer itself, and calcium are all required for optimal receptor activation but none is required for receptor binding.
source: Third, the PtdSer-binding Gla domain of Gas6, PtdSer itself, and calcium are all required for optimal receptor activation but none is required for receptor binding.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Ligand binding does not translate into receptor activation: Gla-less Gas6 binds as well to Axl as does its full-length counterpart, but is dead as an activator.
source: Fourth, ligand binding does not translate into receptor activation: Gla-less Gas6 binds as well to Axl as does its full-length counterpart, but is dead as an activator, and full-length Gas6 binds to Axl in the presence of EDTA but does not activate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Full-length Gas6 binds to Axl in the presence of EDTA but does not activate.
source: Fourth, ligand binding does not translate into receptor activation: Gla-less Gas6 binds as well to Axl as does its full-length counterpart, but is dead as an activator, and full-length Gas6 binds to Axl in the presence of EDTA but does not activate.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figure 4.

claim: Receptor heterodimerization is not an essential feature of TAM activation.
source: Fifth, receptor heterodimerization is not an essential feature of TAM activation, since the TAM receptors can be activated by purified single ligands when expressed as single receptors in MEFs in the absence of any other TAM receptor, and in the retina, Mer activation in wild-type and Tyro3-deficient RPE cells is equivalent.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data in Figures 2 and 7.

claim: In the two settings of PtdSer-dependent 'homeostatic' phagocytosis—by RPE cells in the adult retina and Sertoli cells in the adult testes—Mer is the functionally predominant TAM receptor.
source: Sixth, in the two settings of PtdSer-dependent 'homeostatic' phagocytosis—by RPE cells in the adult retina and Sertoli cells in the adult testes—Mer is the functionally predominant TAM receptor.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic analyses in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In the retina and testes, Pros1 binding to and activation of Mer alone is sufficient to ensure wild-type levels of phagocytosis.
source: And seventh, in these settings, Pros1 binding to and activation of Mer alone is sufficient to ensure wild-type levels of phagocytosis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the genetic analyses in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: A complete TAM signaling module is composed of a receptor, a γ-carboxylated protein ligand, and the phospholipid PtdSer, a tripartite arrangement that is unique to the TAM family.
source: We conclude that a complete TAM signaling module is composed of a receptor, a γ-carboxylated protein ligand, and the phospholipid PtdSer, a tripartite arrangement that is unique to the TAM family.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: The induced exposure of PtdSer is the regulated trigger for TAM activation.
source: Together, all of these observations suggest that the induced exposure of PtdSer is actually the regulated trigger for TAM activation and that the TAM receptor–ligand pair is in reality a PtdSer detector.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the requirement for PtdSer in TAM activation.

claim: The TAM receptor–ligand pair is in reality a PtdSer detector.
source: Together, all of these observations suggest that the induced exposure of PtdSer is actually the regulated trigger for TAM activation and that the TAM receptor–ligand pair is in reality a PtdSer detector.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing the requirement for PtdSer in TAM activation.

claim: An effective TAM signaling complex in vivo is always tripartite, composed of a TAM receptor, a Gla domain-containing TAM ligand, and the phospholipid PtdSer.
source: We propose that an effective TAM signaling complex in vivo is always tripartite, in that it is always composed of a TAM receptor, a Gla domain-containing TAM ligand, and the phospholipid PtdSer (Figure 9). This configuration is unique to the TAMs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data.

claim: All settings of TAM-dependent 'homeostatic phagocytosis' are strictly co-dependent upon the exposure of PtdSer on the surface of the phagocytic target.
source: In this regard, it is important to note that all settings of TAM-dependent 'homeostatic phagocytosis' are strictly co-dependent upon the exposure of PtdSer on the surface of the phagocytic target (Shiratsuchi et al., 1997; Ruggiero et al., 2012; Lemke, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In the case of RPE cell phagocytosis of juxtaposed PR outer segment tips, PtdSer is locally exposed only on these outer segment tips and only during the narrow window after subjective dawn in which phagocytosis occurs each day.
source: In the case of RPE cell phagocytosis of juxtaposed PR outer segment tips, PtdSer is locally exposed only on these outer segment tips (i.e., not on the remainder of the photoreceptor) and only during the narrow window after subjective dawn in which phagocytosis occurs each day (Ruggiero et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The activity of Gla domains is Ca2+-dependent, as these ions both stabilize the folded structure of the domain and also interact with PtdSer.
source: The activity of Gla domains is also Ca2+-dependent, as these ions both stabilize the folded structure of the domain and also interact with PtdSer (Bandyopadhyay, 2008; Huang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The TAM receptor tyrosine kinases represent a novel addition to the set of enzymes whose activities are regulated by both calcium and lipid binding.
source: Thus, the TAM receptor tyrosine kinases represent a novel addition to the set of enzymes, such as protein kinase C, whose activities are regulated by both calcium and lipid binding (Lemmon, 2008; Leonard and Hurley, 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data and comparison to other known systems.

claim: The key difference for the TAMs is that neither the lipid nor the calcium binds the kinase directly; instead, they bind the TAM ligands, which are outside the cell.
source: The key difference for the TAMs is that neither the lipid nor the calcium binds the kinase directly. Instead, they bind the TAM ligands, which are outside the cell.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: All of the very low level of Gas6 that is present in blood appears to be complexed with soluble Axl extracellular domain.
source: The dependence of Axl on Gas6 may be relevant to the fact that all of the very low level of Gas6 that is present in blood appears to be complexed with soluble Axl (sAxl) extracellular domain (Ekman et al., 2010c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Upon Axl activation, the Axl 'ectodomain' is proteolytically cleaved from the rest of the receptor, resulting in the generation of an sAxl–Gas6 complex.
source: Upon Axl activation, this 'ectodomain' is proteolytically cleaved from the rest of the receptor (Costa et al., 1996; O'Bryan et al., 1995; Wilhelm et al., 2008), which results in the generation of an sAxl–Gas6 complex.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The sAxl–Gas6 complex is generated when Axl is activated in tissues subsequent to the injection of activating (cross-linking) α-Axl antibodies.
source: In related work, we have shown that this complex is also generated when Axl is activated in tissues subsequent to the injection of activating (cross-linking) α-Axl antibodies (Zagórska et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to related work.

claim: Antibody depletion of Gas6 from serum does not alter the gel filtration profile of either soluble Mer or Tyro3.
source: Although there are conflicting reports as to the presence of soluble Tyro3 and Mer ectodomains in serum and the possibility that Gas6 might also be bound to soluble Mer (Sather et al., 2007; Ekman et al., 2010c), antibody depletion of Gas6 from serum does not alter the gel filtration profile of either soluble Mer or Tyro3 (Ekman et al., 2010c).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Elevated blood levels of soluble Axl have been reported to mark a variety of human disease and trauma states.
source: Elevated blood levels of soluble Axl have recently been reported to mark a variety of human disease and trauma states, including aortic aneurysm (Ekman et al., 2010b), lupus flares (Zhu et al., 2014), pneumonia infection (Ko et al., 2014), preeclampsia (Liu et al., 2014), coronary bypass (Lee et al., 2013), obesity and insulin resistance (Hsiao et al., 2013), and limb ischemia (Ekman et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The generation of a soluble Axl–Gas6 complex is triggered by the induced cellular exposure of PtdSer in many disease settings.
source: We suggest that the generation of a soluble Axl–Gas6 complex is triggered by the induced cellular exposure of PtdSer in many of these settings.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data and disease associations.

claim: Aberrant TAM signaling in human disease, most notably in cancer, is now a major research focus.
source: Aberrant TAM signaling in human disease, most notably in cancer, is now a major research focus (Leconet et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2013; Schlegel et al., 2013), and small-molecule TAM tyrosine kinase inhibitors and antibodies that inhibit TAM ligand–receptor binding are in development as cancer therapies (Holland et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2010; Brandao et al., 2011; Schlegel et al., 2013; Paccez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Small-molecule TAM tyrosine kinase inhibitors and antibodies that inhibit TAM ligand–receptor binding are in development as cancer therapies.
source: Aberrant TAM signaling in human disease, most notably in cancer, is now a major research focus (Leconet et al., 2013; Meyer et al., 2013; Schlegel et al., 2013), and small-molecule TAM tyrosine kinase inhibitors and antibodies that inhibit TAM ligand–receptor binding are in development as cancer therapies (Holland et al., 2010; Ye et al., 2010; Brandao et al., 2011; Schlegel et al., 2013; Paccez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: TAM inhibitors have been proposed for the treatment of enveloped virus infections.
source: These same inhibitors have been proposed for the treatment of enveloped virus infections (Bhattacharyya et al., 2013; Shibata et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TAM activators have been proposed as possible treatments for several autoimmune indications.
source: Conversely, TAM activators have been proposed as possible treatments for several autoimmune indications (Rothlin and Lemke, 2010; van den Brand et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Tumors profiled in the TCGA database that exhibit mutation or expression changes in the Tyro3, Axl, and Mertk genes display a strong tendency towards mutually exclusive TAM changes across tumor types.
source: In each of these settings, our results indicate that it will be critical to know which TAM receptor to target. This will be particularly important in the context of cancer, since tumors profiled in the TCGA database (https://tcga-data.nci.nih.gov/tcga/) that exhibit mutation or expression changes in the Tyro3, Axl, and Mertk genes display a strong tendency towards mutually exclusive TAM changes across tumor types.
evidence: This is based on analysis of TCGA database data.

claim: Distinct normal functions are preferentially assumed by individual TAM receptors and ligands in macrophages, dendritic cells, Sertoli cells, endothelial cells, and RPE cells.
source: At the same time, our studies here, related work in the immune system (Zagórska et al., 2014), and prior analyses (Scott et al., 2001; Rothlin et al., 2007; Seitz et al., 2007; Burstyn-Cohen et al., 2009, 2012; Carrera Silva et al., 2013) all demonstrate that distinct normal functions are preferentially assumed by individual TAM receptors and ligands in macrophages, dendritic cells, Sertoli cells, endothelial cells, and RPE cells.
evidence: This is supported by the current study and multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The delineation of the rules of engagement for TAM signaling has important implications for the therapeutic application of inhibiting and activating TAM modulators, particularly with respect to their target specificity and the avoidance of possible treatment side effects in the immune, visual, and reproductive systems.
source: Our delineation of the rules of engagement for TAM signaling (Figure 9) therefore has important implications for the therapeutic application of inhibiting and activating TAM modulators, particularly with respect to their target specificity and the avoidance of possible treatment side effects in the immune, visual, and reproductive systems.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the implications of the study findings.
